summary: For ages 9–11, teach relative dating as reading a sequence of rock strata: order layers by the law of superposition (undisturbed: deeper = older, higher = younger), correlate layers between separated sites using index fossils, then handle real-world disruptions (tilting/folding, faults, intrusions, unconformities) so the rule is understood with its conditions. The core objective is reconstructing a SEQUENCE OF EVENTS from the evidence — for example deposition, then deformation, then erosion, with features that cut across layers being younger than those layers — and distinguishing relative dating (order) from absolute dating (a number of years).
misconceptions: 'The bottom layer is always oldest, no matter what' — tilting, folding and faulting can overturn or rearrange sequences.
'Rock layers tell you exact ages in years' — relative dating gives order only, not numeric age.
'A gap in layers means nothing happened' — an unconformity represents missing/eroded time.
'Layers formed at the slope they're now tilted to' — by original horizontality, they formed flat and were tilted later.
'Matching rock type proves same age' — correlation relies on index fossils/markers, since similar rock can form at different times.

activities.title: Build the cliff, then correlate two sites, then read the disruptions
steps: Arrange labelled sediment layers (e.g. sand, mud, ash) into the order they were deposited, and check them against the law of superposition — the deepest layer settled first, so bottom = oldest, top = youngest.

Look at a second outcrop a valley away with no obvious link; find the SAME distinctive index fossil appearing in a band of each cliff and draw a correlation line connecting those bands, so two separate cliffs tell one shared story.

Introduce complications one at a time: tilt the beds onto their side, push a sheet of magma (an igneous intrusion, which cools underground) up through the layers, or cut a fault across them — then reconstruct the ORDER OF EVENTS from the evidence: layers must exist before they can be tilted, and anything that cuts across layers (a fault or an intrusion) is younger than the layers it cuts. For example: layers deposited, THEN tilted, THEN cut by an intrusion — but if a fault breaks through the intrusion, the fault came last.

Identify an unconformity (a buried erosion surface — often uneven, or with layers at different angles above and below it) and state that it represents a gap in the record where rock was eroded away or never deposited, not 'nothing happened'.
State explicitly whether your reading gives an order only or an exact age in years.
activities.insight: Rocks record a sequence of happenings you read like a diary, not just a stack you count from the bottom. Superposition (deeper = older) holds for undisturbed layers; tilting, faulting and intrusions can reorient, rearrange or cut across layers, so you must reconstruct the sequence of events rather than assume the simple rule. Index fossils let you line up distant outcrops, and relative dating gives order only — not a numeric age.

activities.title: Annotated strata cliff: vocabulary and the basic reading
steps: Examine a labelled strata cliff cross-section and reveal, for each band, its relative age position and any index fossils it contains.
Reveal the meaning of the marked erosion-surface contact line: 'unconformity — a gap in the record where rock was eroded away or never deposited'.
Say, in your own words, which layer formed first and why.
activities.insight: The vocabulary of strata reading — superposition, index fossil, unconformity — attached to a concrete labelled cross-section, so the basic 'bottom-is-oldest' reading and its key terms are secure before ordering and disruption practice.

activities.title: Check the reading: order, matching and which-formed-first
steps: Put five labelled layers into order oldest → youngest.
Answer which layer formed first in a given undisturbed cliff.
Match a shared index fossil across two columns — e.g. link layer B at site 1 to layer D at site 2 — to show the two outcrops correlate.
activities.insight: Checks whether the learner can read a sequence and use index fossils to correlate sites, surfacing confusions such as reversing the order or relying on rock type instead of fossils.

activities.title: Optional extension: rotate and slice a 3D geological block
steps: Rotate a geological block model to view the strata from different angles.
Slice the block along a chosen plane to expose the internal layers and a fault surface.
Describe how the tilt or fault reads differently when seen in three dimensions versus a flat cross-section.
activities.insight: Strata are genuinely three-dimensional; viewing and slicing a rotatable block can make a tilt or fault surface easier to see for the disruption cases.

checkQuestion: In a cliff, one fossil is found in a deep low layer of rock and another in a high layer near the top. Which fossil is older — and does looking at the layers tell you exactly how many years old it is? Explain.
checkAnswer: The fossil in the deeper, lower layer is older, because sediment layers build up with the oldest at the bottom and the youngest on top. But the layers only tell you the ORDER (which is older or younger), not an exact age in years — you'd need another method, such as radiometric dating, for an actual number.
